title: Race Conditions
description: TOCTOU bugs, the ABA problem, memory ordering on x86 vs ARM, Java happens-before semantics, and Go's data race detector.

segments.text: Race conditions are the most dangerous class of bugs in production. They're non-deterministic, nearly impossible to reproduce in testing, and can cause data corruption that goes undetected for weeks. This lesson covers the patterns behind race conditions and the tools that catch them.

A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location, at least one is a write, and there's no synchronization. The result depends on execution order, which the OS scheduler controls. The same code can run correctly 999,999 times and fail on the millionth run. This is why code review and testing alone don't catch race conditions.

TOCTOU — time of check, time of use — is a race between checking a condition and acting on it. Classic example: check if a file exists, then open it. Between the check and the open, another process deletes the file. In security, this enables symlink attacks: check permissions on a file, attacker swaps it with a symlink to /etc/passwd, then you read the wrong file.

In web applications, TOCTOU appears everywhere. Check inventory, then create order — between check and create, another request buys the last item. Check balance, then debit — another transaction debits first. The solution is atomic operations: compare-and-swap at the CPU level, or SELECT FOR UPDATE at the database level.

The ABA problem is subtle. Thread one reads value A, gets preempted. Thread two changes value to B, then back to A. Thread one resumes, sees A, assumes nothing changed. But the state may have changed and reverted. In lock-free data structures, this causes corruption. The fix is version counters: stamp each value with a monotonically increasing version.
segments.thought_prompt: In a lock-free linked list, how could the ABA problem cause a node to point to freed memory?

segments.text: Modern CPUs reorder instructions for performance. x86 uses Total Store Ordering — stores are seen in program order by other cores, but loads can be reordered before stores. ARM uses weak ordering — almost everything can be reordered. A correctly synchronized program on x86 can have data races on ARM because x86 hides them with its stronger guarantees.

Memory barriers, or fences, prevent the CPU from reordering across the barrier. A store fence ensures all prior stores are visible before subsequent stores. An acquire fence prevents loads from being moved before the acquire. Release fences prevent stores from being moved after the release. This is what volatile in Java and atomic operations in C++ compile down to.

Java's happens-before relationship defines when one thread's writes are guaranteed visible to another. Unlocking a monitor happens-before locking the same monitor. Writing to a volatile field happens-before reading it. Starting a thread happens-before any action in that thread. If there's no happens-before chain, the JVM can show you stale values — even values that were never written.

Go's race detector instruments memory accesses at compile time and detects concurrent unsynchronized access at runtime. Run your tests with go test dash race. It has roughly 10x runtime overhead, so don't use it in production. But in CI, it catches races that would take months to manifest in production. At Google, the race detector found thousands of bugs across their Go codebase.

ThreadSanitizer, or TSan, does for C and C++ what the Go race detector does for Go. It uses shadow memory to track which thread last accessed each memory location. When it detects unsynchronized concurrent access, it reports the exact lines of code and the two conflicting threads. LLVM and GCC both support it natively.

A war story: a payment service had a race condition in its idempotency check. Two requests with the same idempotency key arrived within microseconds. Both checked the database, found no existing record, and both processed the payment. The customer was charged twice. The fix: a unique constraint on the idempotency key column with retry logic on constraint violation.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is a database unique constraint better than an application-level check for idempotency?

segments.text: Race conditions are not random bugs — they're design flaws. Use atomic operations for simple shared state. Use proper synchronization for complex invariants. Run race detectors in CI. And remember: if you can't prove your code is race-free through happens-before analysis, it probably isn't. The CPU will find the race condition before you do.
